documents: Endut et al. (2022) Texture and morphology of veins and their relationship to gold mineralization in the Penjom deposit, Malaysia. Resource Geology 72:e12288, published PDF (18 pp.)
pages_convention: printed journal pages (article pages '1 of 18' to '18 of 18', identical to PDF pages counted from 1)

entry.evidence: investigated based on macroscopic and microscopic characteristics to understand the process of veins formation, and the relationship with gold mineralization

sequences.source_document: Endut et al. 2022, Resource Geology, published PDF

steps.action: States the aim: describe Penjom vein textures from hand specimens and thin sections to understand vein formation, structural timing and the relation to gold content.
steps.quote: to understand the process of veins formation, and the relationship with gold mineralization

steps.action: Takes over the authors' earlier structural framework (D1-D5 deformation phases, vein styles, galena geochemistry; Endut et al. 2015a, 2015b; Endut 2016), restated in Sections 1.1-1.3 and Table 2.
steps.quote: Structural control of veins in Penjom has been discussed in Endut et al. (2015a)

steps.action: Adopts published texture classifications (Dowling & Morrison 1989; Vearncombe 1993) that link quartz textures to growth direction, stress regime and crustal depth, giving the expectations used to read the textures.
steps.quote: Vearncombe (1993) classified the veins based on the growth direction of the quartz and interpretation toward the depth of formation.

steps.action: Uses vein exposures that became available at mining faces and interim pit walls during mining, across almost all orebodies.
steps.quote: The availability of good exposures is the main criterion of this study's success.

steps.action: Collects representative samples of each texture and prepares five thin sections cut perpendicular to vein strike, from the main shear and from massive extensional or thick shear veins.
steps.quote: The samples were cut perpendicular to the strike of the vein so that the whole spectrum of quartz grains across the shear could be observed.

steps.action: Describes and classifies macroscopic textures into primary (buck, comb, laminae) and secondary (ribbon, breccia, stylolite, spider veinlet) and records cross-cutting relations (Figures 3-5).
steps.quote: Two major textural groups can be recognized based on grain morphology in the veins using both the naked eye and microscope.

steps.action: Describes microtextures in thin section (buck grain size, comb c-axes, polygonal subgrains, undulose extinction, sutured and bulging grains, cataclasite) and measures c-axis orientations and lengths of 34 grains (Figure 6).
steps.quote: Subsequent infiltration and crystallization along active margins resulted in grain size reduction to form secondary polygonal subgrains

steps.action: Infers stress and pressure conditions of vein formation (confining pressure, dilation, crack-seal, pressure solution) from grain shapes, using the cited texture criteria.
steps.quote: Buck texture implies high confining pressure where anhedral grain shape points to compressional force and euhedral grain shape indicate tensional force

steps.action: Compares textures with the gold grades in Table 2: buck quartz is low grade unless overprinted, while ribbon, laminated and breccia textures carry medium to very high grades.
steps.quote: The D2 buck quartz is low in content of gold unless it is overprinted by deformation

steps.action: Compares the association of ribbon and laminated textures with high grade to other mesozonal vein-type gold deposits worldwide.
steps.quote: This is also common in other mesozonal vein-type gold deposits worldwide

steps.action: Assigns deformation temperatures to the microstructures using published ranges (undulose extinction below 300 C, sutured grains 300-500 C, BLG recrystallization 250-400 C).
steps.quote: new subgrain may have formed through the process of bulging re-crystallization (BLG), which is also at low temperature at around 250–400C

steps.action: Checks the field-based phase sequence against grain-scale microtextures, which show at least two progressive deformation phases (late folding and faulting, then post-mineralization).
steps.quote: Microtextures study of the quartz grains supports the evidence on microscopic grain scale of at least two progressive structural deformation phases

steps.action: Relates the siting of visible gold (ribbon texture, vein margins, breccia aggregates) and its cross-cutting by spider veinlets to the D2-D3 fault reactivation history.
steps.quote: In shear veins, visible gold is commonly hosted within the ribbon texture (Figure 8a)

steps.action: States two published accounts of gold timing: early deposition followed by remobilization, versus introduction during multiple veining episodes.
steps.quote: Gold can also be introduced during multiple episodes of veining, fluid flow and deposition in favorable sites

steps.action: Keeps a two-episode gold model (D2 folding with ribbon and laminated textures; D3 brecciation) that is consistent with both accounts, summarized in the Figure 9 paragenesis, with D4 spider veinlets post-dating gold.
steps.quote: Gold mineralization in Penjom implies both interpretations and temporal relationships to the fold and fault activities

steps.action: Concludes that the Penjom texture suite resembles slate-belt and mesozonal orogenic lode gold deposits.
steps.quote: Textural study at Penjom shows similarity with slate belt or mesozonal orogenic lode gold

tree.answer: Quartz vein textures and their association with gold at Penjom
Textures yes; formation conditions and timing only through traces
Understand vein formation and its relation to gold mineralization episodes
Only cited rivals for gold timing (early deposition with remobilization vs multiple episodes)
No distinct predictions derived; both rivals are judged compatible
Conditions found: mine exposures and five thin sections
Microtextures said to support the phase sequence; no independent data or variation
Two gold episodes (D2, D3) kept as an interpretation

end.claim: Gold at Penjom was emplaced in two episodes, during D2 folding (ribbon and laminated textures) and D3 fault reactivation and brecciation; primary buck quartz is gold-poor unless overprinted, and D4 spider veinlets post-date mineralization.

decisive_move.sentence: Relating texture types and cross-cutting relations to gold siting and grade (Table 2, Figures 5 and 8) is what ties the texture classification to gold mineralization episodes.

gates.evidence: Sampling followed the availability of mine exposures ('The availability of good exposures is the main criterion', p. 7), not a stated hypothesis. The gold-timing model is declared compatible with both cited accounts (p. 15), not exposed to a test that could fail. Nothing was fixed in advance.

imports.item: Electron probe microanalysis (EPMA) of gold grain composition (cited from Abdul Aziz 2013)
LA-ICP-MS trace-element analysis of galena (cited from Endut et al. 2015b)

limits: The microscopic basis is small: five thin sections (p. 7), and a c-axis plot of 34 grains from one area. The source and assay method of the gold grades in Table 2 are not stated (inference: mine assay data or Endut 2016). No quantitative test links texture to grade. The cited rivals for gold timing are not discriminated; both are accepted. Sub-claims and statuses: formation conditions from textures (confining pressure, crack-seal), best_explanation by analogy with Dowling & Morrison and Vearncombe criteria. Deformation temperatures, estimate taken from literature ranges with no resolution derived here. The link to the Late Triassic-Early Jurassic orogeny rests on an inherited, unpublished sericite age (Bogie 2003) and earlier structural work, not on new dating. The acknowledgments mention an editor, an associate editor and two anonymous reviewers, but no review file was supplied, so the changes made in review cannot be coded. Data are available only on request. The trace_series composition is a loose fit: the paper is largely descriptive and its rivals are barely stated (inference).

disagreements.target: Dowling and Morrison (1989) description of infill breccia texture
disagreements.support: In Penjom infill breccias the later-phase fluid carried an insoluble carbon residue rather than silica, from hand-specimen and thin-section observation.
disagreements.quote: These characteristics are slightly different from the description of Dowling and Morrison (1989), which considers silica fluid as a later phase.

alternatives_considered.chosen: Breccia texture as deformation features within the vein (infill and aggregate subclasses)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: undeformed hydrothermal breccias; deformed fault breccias
alternatives_considered.reason: fault breccia is characterized by angular host rock fragments in a fault zone

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both interpretations (early gold remobilized, plus introduction during multiple episodes) tied to D2 and D3
alternatives_considered.alternatives: early deposition with later remobilization (Mumin et al. 1994; Davis and Hippert 1998; Groves et al. 2003); multiple episodes of veining and deposition (Oberthür et al. 1997)
alternatives_considered.reason: none given beyond stating that Penjom 'implies both interpretations'
